title: Extracellular matrix regulates lineage plasticity in prostate cancer through YAP/TEAD
abstract: Treatment-related neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) is an increasingly frequent mechanism of resistance to androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) therapy in prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD). This lineage transition is dependent on upregulation of the NE-specifying transcription factor ASCL1, typically in a genetic background of RB1 and TP53 loss. Here we identify extracellular matrix-integrin-YAP1/TEAD signaling as a critical brake on NEPC lineage transition. Deletion of Itgb1, the shared B1 subunit required for collagen and laminin-mediated integrin activation, is sufficient to induce ASCL1 and NE lineage gene expression, by activating LATS1/2 kinases with subsequent inactivation of YAP1/TEAD signaling. Conversely, restoration of YAP1/TEAD signaling by pharmacological LATS1/2 inhibition, or by expression of constitutively active YAP1/TAZ mutants, prevents or reverts NEPC lineage transition. NOTCH and AR cooperate with YAP/TEAD to repress ASCL1, such that combined inhibition leads to complete reprograming of PRAD into NEPC in vitro, providing a dynamic platform to dissect the molecular events responsible for lineage transition over time. We find that lineage transition is accompanied by a redistribution of FOXA1 and TEAD cistromes from PRAD to NEPC-specific enhancers and requires the pioneering activity of FOXA1. Thus, extracellular matrix/integrin signaling in the PRAD tumor microenvironment restrains NE lineage plasticity, highlighting a potential path for pharmacological inhibitors in modulating treatment-induced lineage change.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This preprint has already begun to shape follow-on prostate cancer research. The record shows early downstream reuse in two later works, alongside a scite profile that includes one supporting citation statement and three additional mentions. That pattern suggests the study’s central idea—linking extracellular matrix and YAP/TEAD signaling to lineage plasticity in treatment-related neuroendocrine prostate cancer—is being read as a meaningful mechanistic contribution, even though the citation base is still small.

Full narrative

The article argues that extracellular matrix–integrin–YAP1/TEAD signaling acts as a brake on neuroendocrine lineage transition in prostate cancer, adding a new layer to the biology of treatment resistance. In the broader context of ARPI-resistant disease and ASCL1-driven lineage switching, that framing is likely to be of interest to researchers studying how microenvironmental cues constrain or enable plasticity.

Evidence of uptake is still early, but it is not absent. OpenAlex currently shows three citations in 2026, and the citing literature is squarely in prostate cancer research, including a review on molecular profiling for castration-resistant prostate cancer and a Nature Reviews Urology article on disrupted integrin signaling and neuroendocrine differentiation. A related bioRxiv preprint on MYC pathway reprogramming in neuroendocrine lineage transition also cites the work, indicating that the paper is already feeding into active mechanistic discussion.

The reuse record reinforces that picture. Two downstream works are documented as reusing the article, including an article indexed by Europe PMC and a later journal article in Neoplasia. Scite also registers one supporting citation statement and three mentioning statements, which is consistent with a nascent but real footprint in the literature rather than a fully matured citation history.

The stewardship signals point to substantial research backing, with support from major biomedical funders including NCI, NIH, HHMI, and Calico Life Sciences. The paper is also associated with Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and HHMI contributors, aligning it with a high-profile cancer biology research environment. Overall, the record shows an early-stage but credible influence: the paper is being cited, reused, and discussed within the prostate cancer field, especially around lineage plasticity, extracellular matrix biology, and neuroendocrine differentiation.
